passage: Tuesday Dear Diary, Ishita didn't play dog-and-bone again. When the whistle went she walked to the far bench with her hands over her ears. Priyal said she's snobby. I don't think so. At lunch Ishita told me the whole route of the night train to Guwahati, every station, without stopping. I didn't understand half, but her eyes went shiny. So today I asked her, "Do you want to play something, or is the bench better?" She said, "Can we play trains?" We drew a timetable game in chalk. I was the passenger, she was the station master. Three more girls joined. Ishita laughed so loud! Tomorrow she's bringing her train cards. - Kavitha

qa.q: Which train's route did Ishita describe at lunch?
qa.a: The night train to Guwahati, every station, without stopping.

qa.q: What does Kavitha think about Priyal calling Ishita snobby?
qa.a: Kavitha doesn't agree and seems to think Ishita avoids the game for another reason, like the noise, not because she is proud.

qa.q: Which choice by Kavitha opened up a real friendship?
qa.a: Kavitha asked Ishita what she wanted instead of assuming, then played a train game built around Ishita's interest.

qa.q: How might Ishita see break time differently after the chalk timetable game?
qa.a: Break may feel like a place where she belongs, since others joined a game she loves and she laughed out loud.

grounding: A classmate notices a peer who avoids loud games and talks a lot about trains, asks instead of assuming, and includes her through her interest.

passage: During games period at the government school, some boys yelled "Train-wali!" as Pallavi slipped away from the noisy kabaddi circle. The new girl, Lalremsiami, watched her sit under the neem tree, counting on her fingers: engine, eleven wagons, guard van. Instead of guessing, Lalremsiami sat down a little distance away. "Do you want company, or quiet?" Pallavi thought. "Company. But no shouting." "Which train comes past here at four?" Pallavi's whole face opened. She explained the goods train with cement wagons and why it always waits at the signal. After school they stood at the level crossing and counted the wagons out loud together. Next day, when someone called "Train-wali" again, Lalremsiami said, "She knows more than the stationmaster," and kept walking beside her.

qa.q: What was Pallavi counting on her fingers under the neem tree?
How did Lalremsiami seem to feel about Pallavi, and how can you tell she did not want to assume what Pallavi needed?
qa.a: She seemed curious and caring; she sat a little distance away and asked, 'Do you want company, or quiet?' instead of guessing.

qa.q: What turning point changed the teasing on the second day?
qa.a: Lalremsiami refused to join in, answered the teasing calmly and kept walking beside Pallavi.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel when Lalremsiami asks about the four o'clock train?
qa.a: Pallavi likely felt seen and happy; her whole face opened, and she gladly explained the goods train.

grounding: A classmate notices a girl who avoids loud games and talks about trains, asks instead of assuming, does not tease and builds friendship around her interest.
